Iran says it targeted US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike
First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s first direct attack on US military installations for months.
“This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”
US Central Command denied that the radar system had been destroyed and said US forces had intercepted two Iranian drones headed for Bahrain .
Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews over the past 24 hours that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia, have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes.
Trump said he had asked the vice-president, JD Vance, to end his interest in negotiating a new deal with Iran and instead focus on corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.
Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal.
Vance has been at the forefront of Republicans saying the war was the cause of the widespread Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public because higher diesel prices were a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
An opinion poll in the UK showed 65% of the British public would oppose the US resuming the war in Iran, and only 14% would back it. The poll was conducted by YouGov for the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu).
It also found 54% oppose UK bases being used by the US to mount attacks on Iran, with 29% in favour. Support for additional UK sanctions against Iran was 45%, with 22% opposed.
The poll was conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, before two Iranians were found guilty on Thursday of spying and planning attacks on journalists in the UK. The Iranian embassy has rejected the court judgment as an attempt to advance a political agenda.
Chris Doyle, the director of Caabu, said: “The British public are sceptical about any war on Iran and what it might achieve. What might make the Burnham government take note is the very high level of opposition to any further war amongst 2024 Labour voters, at 79%.”
Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a body of elected Islamic jurists responsible for choosing the supreme leader, has become the first governing institution in Iran to call for a review of the country’s defence doctrine, potentially leading to religious permission for Iran to try to acquire a nuclear weapon.
In a statement released on Thursday, the assembly called for a review of Iran’s membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, describing the move as an “unavoidable necessity” and a “public and national demand”.
The intervention carries a religious as much as political significance because the 88-strong assembly comprises senior clerics, most of whom are supposed to be qualified to exercise independent Islamic legal reasoning.
Iran has had a longstanding prohibition on nuclear weapons, based on a fatwa issued by the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, but the relevance of the fatwa in the wake of the US attacks on Iran has been questioned widely in political and security circles.
Whether Iran has the stockpiles of uranium or technology to build a nuclear weapon is contested.
The UN nuclear inspectorate has expressed alarm about a continued lack of information from Iran about its nuclear sites. It said: “Our concerns are growing over Iran’s refusal to allow access to design information or inspections of the Isfahan facility. We do not know the exact location of the Isfahan uranium enrichment facility or whether it contains nuclear materials. It is imperative that we carry out our verification activities in Iran without further delay.”

A tanker carrying liquefied gas hit a mine and suffered an explosion on Friday while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz via a route not authorized by Iran, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said .
The vessel was using an "unauthorised and dangerous route" in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iran's state media cited by Reuters.
The attacks on vessels carrying energy products through the Strait of Hormuz have intensified in the past month, with Iran reporting incidents nearly every day.
On Thursday, the Iranian military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz. The tankers had ignored warnings from Iran and entered restricted areas of the Strait, Tehran said, as it remains defiant that it controls transits.
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's top negotiator and Parliament Speaker, told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz navigation would not return to pre-war conditions, ever.
"There are no 'free waters' [international waters] there, and the 1982 [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] does not apply to the strait … The regulations within the Strait of Hormuz are governed by the laws of the two littoral states that border it," the official told Al Jazeera.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Thursday, "We don't need a deal with Iran" and that "Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!"
Friday's mine-and-explosion incident with the LNG vessel comes days after Kpler data showed that exports of liquefied natural gas via the Strait of Hormuz last month reached the highest total since February , at 31 tankers, compared with 23 in September.
Despite the increase in loadings, the total from Qatar is far from pre-war levels. According to Kpler, LNG loadings at Qatar's Ras Laffan terminal exceeded 2.7 million tons in October, while the country exported nearly 6.2 million tons in February.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent attends a bilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump and Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City, US, September 22, 2026. [Kylie Cooper/Reuters]
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called on the Federal Reserve not to hike interest rates because of an “energy supply shock” tied to the US-led conflict with Iran.
“I think the Fed should understand that this is an energy supply shock,” while the underlying US economy is very strong, Bessent said in an interview on CNBC on Friday.

“So I think that to hike too much into an energy supply shock when it’s coming down, these are very noisy numbers,” he said. “The Fed’s supposed to look into the future, not look in the rearview mirror.”
The central bank opted to maintain interest rates during its last policy meeting, leaving them at 3.75 to 4 percent. CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, forecasts an 89.4 percent chance that rates will be raised to 4.00–4.25 percent at the next meeting, scheduled for December 9.
Despite pressure from the White House to cut interest rates, the Federal Reserve has held them steady amid inflationary pressures stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran . Since the conflict began, the Fed has maintained rates five times and raised them once.
Much of that pressure has come from rising energy prices. By September, energy prices had climbed 20.4 percent year over year. Although October’s energy price data has since been released, the Labour Department was unable to collect data in October 2025 because of last year’s government shutdown. As a result, it cannot provide a year-over-year comparison for October 2026.
Bessent’s remarks come amid a stronger-than-expected US jobs report, which bolsters the case for rate hikes. The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, according to the Labour Department’s release last Friday.
“I’m not going to tell the Fed what to do. I am going to say they should have an open mind,” Bessent said.
The Fed made three rate cuts over the same period last year, he noted.
“And now to reverse just based on an energy supply shock, a reversal in a dramatic way isn’t something that I would do if I were on the Fed. But I’m not on the Fed.”
Bessent’s remarks come as some top Fed officials are pushing for the opposite. On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he planned to support a quarter-point increase at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting unless the core consumer price index — one of the central bank’s key measures for assessing the rate of inflation — came in at 0.3 percent or more.
“In that case, I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting,” he said at a conference in London hosted by King’s Business School and the Money Macro and Finance Society.
The CPI report subsequently came out, showing a 0.4 percent monthly increase.
Consumers are feeling the rising costs at the petrol pump, as prices are declining but remain high. The average price for a gallon of petrol is $3.87 ($1.02 per litre), down from $4.34 ($1.14 per litre)this time a month ago, but still well above the $2.98 ($0.79 per litre) price recorded on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.

Iraq’s Oil Production Soars to 2019 High as Hormuz Flows Surge
Iraq's crude oil production hit 4.6 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, the highest since 2019, data from the International Energy Agency's monthly report showed on Friday, as OPEC's second-largest producer hiked output by 540,000 bpd from September.
Kuwait and Saudi Arabia also boosted their October crude oil output compared to September, as rising volumes of oil are leaving the Strait of Hormuz on smaller tankers, which then transfer the crude cargoes onto supertankers in the Gulf of Oman.
Iraq's October crude oil production topped its OPEC+ quota by about 170,000 bpd, showed the data in the IEA's Oil Market Report for November.
Kuwait also boosted its crude oil production last month, from 1.58 million bpd in September to 2.03 million bpd in October, although the Gulf producer was still about 650,000 bpd short of its OPEC+ ceiling.
OPEC's top producer and de facto leader, Saudi Arabia, hiked crude oil production by about 1 million bpd to 9.99 million bpd, up from 8.93 million bpd in September, according to IEA data.
Per the agency's estimates, Saudi Arabia was still producing 480,000 bpd below its OPEC+ quota in October.
The Kingdom told OPEC that it pumped 10.563 million bpd in October , back near pre-war levels and slightly above its OPEC+ quota of about 10.5 million bpd. The Saudis, however, noted in OPEC's monthly report that part of the jump in output went straight into storage, which means Saudi supply to the market for exports didn't soar as much as production did.
Saudi Arabia's supply to the market (domestic and overseas) was 7.122 million bpd in August, 7.988 million bpd in September, and 9.2 million bpd in October, while production was 6.238 million bpd in August, rising to 8.372 million bpd in September, and to 10.563 million bpd in October.
Gulf producers have ramped up crude oil production in recent weeks as crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have significantly increased since August, thanks to shuttle shipments through the chokepoint.

Malaysia and Singapore have intensified scrutiny of AI hardware shipments amid concerns about the potential circumvention of U.S. export restrictions on China. Malaysia has launched an investigation into whether AI hardware imported by a subsidiary of the ill-fated Megaspeed was subsequently exported to other countries, reports Reuters . Meanwhile, Singapore has charged another executive over questionable purchases of 917 servers that may contain Nvidia accelerators, according to The Straits Times . The news follows the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang over claims he had multiple extra-marital affairs , including with a possible Chinese intelligence asset who facilitated GPU smuggling into China. Analysts speculate that systematic chip smuggling may be the reason behind his departure .

Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry is examining whether Speedmatrix, the Malaysian subsidiary of Singapore-based Megaspeed , re-exported any of the AI processors and servers it had imported for use in local data centers. Apparently, after months of investigating, authorities have yet to find out whether any such shipments occurred and, if they did, whether they complied with Malaysian laws. Malaysia introduced restrictions on the export, transit, and trans-shipment of advanced U.S.-developed AI accelerators in July 2025, so it now requires companies to obtain appropriate permits.
The Malaysian ministry said it was cooperating with customs authorities as well as officials in Singapore and the U.S., and could introduce additional restrictions. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said there was no evidence that Megaspeed-related AI hardware had left Malaysia, but he promised to cooperate with international investigations.
Speaking of Megaspeed, the company said on November 12 that it had hired a U.S. law firm to conduct a comprehensive inventory of its AI GPUs and independently assess its compliance with U.S. export-control regulations, reports DigiTimes . The company also confirmed that it had cooperated with inspections by the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) and was prepared to cooperate with other U.S. government agencies if necessary.
James Tan Yong Pong, chief executive of Megaspeed, stressed that compliance with U.S. export rules as well as transparent operations were always a priority for the company. However, Megaspeed did not disclose how many GPUs it owns and which GPU models it has, what BIS examined during its inspections, or whether the authorities had identified any violations.
Meanwhile, Singaporean authorities have brought 41 criminal charges against Shi Bingzhe, a 34-year-old Chinese citizen who served as director of Superphi and chief operating officer of NJ Global Financial. The two companies purchased 917 servers containing restricted Nvidia hardware from Aperia International in 41 transactions between May 2024 and February 2025, according to prosecutors. Authorities allege that the companies had reason to believe the servers were linked to criminal activity by Aperia International. Superphi now faces six charges, while NJ Global Financial faces 35.
The latest charges expand a case that now involves five individuals and six companies. Four firms — Aperia International, A-Speed Infotech, Aperia Cloud Services (II), and Luxuriate Your Life — were charged in July over allegedly making false claims when purchasing servers. Meanwhile, the exact nature of those claims was not disclosed in the report. Authorities have frozen the disposal of a property worth approximately S$55 million and confiscated around S$1 million from bank accounts. Shi faces up to 10 years in prison and a fine of S$500,000 per charge if convicted. His next court appearance is scheduled for January 4, 2027.

The two cases largely highlight the significance of Malaysia and Singapore in the supply chain of restricted AI hardware to places where it should not be, such as China. Singapore's investigation focuses on alleged fraud and transactions involving proceeds of criminal activity, whereas Malaysia seeks to find out whether imported AI equipment was subsequently shipped abroad in violation of local regulations.
Neither investigation has found that the hardware ultimately reached China, but both illustrate difficulties that authorities face as they attempt to enforce restrictions on advanced AI hardware across international supply chains.

items.title: Russia is ‘setting traps’ in Ukraine talks, EU foreign policy chief warns - The Guardian
items.summary: Russia is ‘setting traps’ in Ukraine talks, EU foreign policy chief warns  The Guardian
items.content:
Kallas urged leaders at the EU summit in Dublin to ‘keep the focus’. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA
Kallas urged leaders at the EU summit in Dublin to ‘keep the focus’. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA
Russia is ‘setting traps’ in Ukraine talks, EU foreign policy chief warns
Kaja Kallas says Moscow is trying to divert attention from its aggression by raising issue of European security
The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.
“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”
In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US were held this week in Abu Dhabi.
Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.
European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.
Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.
The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.
The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.
Despite more than two years of on-off talks, the EU has not settled on a choice. But there is a growing view that Europe should not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent.
Paris and Berlin support a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: the European Council’s president, António Costa, and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.
Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.
Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”
Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of the coalition of the willing , a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

items.title: Nvidia scandal fallout widens as Trump's treasury secretary blames cabinet colleague
items.summary: Scott Bessent suggests Howard Lutnick’s commerce department failed to ban exports of Nvidia's chips to a firm thought to have links with China.
items.content:
Figure caption, How could the Nvidia CEOâs affair threaten US national security?
By Rachel Clun Business Reporter ,Â  Reporting from New York
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed the Commerce Department, run by Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec Nvidia chips, as the fallout from the scandal widens.
There is growing pressure on Lutnick across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.
Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy.
Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it had been smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but is not on a list of firms that US companies are prevented from working with.
Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.
Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.
Image caption, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said some parts of the administration wanted more controls on trade with Megaspeed
Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.
"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.
There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but separate reporting in the Financial Times said the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.
However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.
"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC's Squawk Box programme , external .
"The real story here should be: Did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?
"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."
How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions
Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.
The Commerce Secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman, Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.
Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E. Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.
According to Neal and Wyden, Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into America for inspection.
A 25% tariff - a levy that is paid to the federal government - was imposed on those chips, under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security.
"Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

items.title: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett’s 6-Word Advice Is the Smartest Move You Can Make - The Motley Fool
items.summary: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett’s 6-Word Advice Is the Smartest Move You Can Make  <font color="#6f6f6f"
items.content:
The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite have both slipped since the start of November, and many investors are uneasy about what comes next.
Warren Buffett's rule of being greedy when others are fearful helped turn his crisis-era investments in Goldman Sachs and Bank of America into billions of dollars in gains.
If stocks keep sliding, I think the move is to keep steadily investing in a diverse set of strong businesses and hold long term, because a market recovery won't lift every stock.
While it's been far from a smooth ride, stock market investors have had plenty of success over the last few years. Behind a booming artificial intelligence trade , the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.47% ) has gained nearly 115% since the fall of 2022, while the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -0.94% ) has jumped more than 150%.
But the last couple of weeks have stung: The S&P 500 is down 3% over the past month, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq is down 7%.
Many investors are uneasy. There's a lot of noise right now . It's natural. So, it seems to me that now is the perfect time to consider some sage advice from one of the most successful investors of all time: Warren Buffett.
Warren Buffett's advice for a stock market crash
Crashes happen in the stock market. They're a fact of life. They cannot be avoided, but what you do -- or don't do -- when one happens makes all the difference in the long run. It turns out that the latter half of one of Buffett's most famous aphorisms is one of the most important pieces of advice to keep in mind.
This simple phrase could help you avoid the costliest mistake you can make during a crash -- panic selling -- while remembering not to overlook the opportunity in front of you: the chance to buy shares of great businesses at a discount.
Buffett himself demonstrated this during the financial crisis. In September 2008, Berkshire Hathaway invested $5 billion in Goldman Sachs , receiving preferred shares paying a 10% dividend and warrants -- which turned into roughly $3.2 billion in profit. Buffett's $5 billion Bank of America investment in the wake of the crisis turned into a $12 billion on-paper profit six years later.
Of course, you have to be careful. Not all stocks are created equal, and crashes tend to weed out companies that weren't sound to begin with. Just because the market as a whole will inevitably recover does not mean that individual stocks will.
It's worth keeping another Buffett quote in mind: "Charlie (Munger) and I are not stock-pickers; we are business-pickers." Investing in companies with durable competitive advantages, good economics that don't implode when the economy slows down or funding dries up, and led by competent leaders will help ensure the stock recovers when the dust settles.
I don't know whether the last couple of weeks are the start of something bigger or just a bump in a long rally -- no one does. But if stocks do keep sliding, keep doing what you were (hopefully) doing before: steadily investing in a diverse set of strong businesses and holding for the long term.

items.title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
items.summary: The fact the question of European security now features in discussions is viewed in Moscow as a victory, BBC Russia Editor Steve Rosenberg says.
items.content:
Image caption, Putin sounded uncompromising and confident at his talks with the US envoys
By Steve Rosenberg Russia Editor ,Â  Reporting from Moscow
Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.
That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.
And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?
The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."
Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.
What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.
The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 â the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.
What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".
That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.
But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.
"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.
"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".
"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."
Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.
Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.
This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.
After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.
But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.
"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
Zelensky welcomes US bringing Europe into Russia-Ukraine peace talks
Europe's security 'fundamentally reshaped' by war in Ukraine
Inside devastated front-line city that Russia wants Ukraine to give up
At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.
The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.
And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.
And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.
Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.
But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

items.title: Why is Ukraine attacking Russian warships in the Baltic Sea amid talks? - Al Jazeera

items.content:
Share Why is Ukraine attacking Russian warships in the Baltic Sea amid talks? on social media
Smoke from a fire rises above the port area of Ust-Luga on the Baltic Sea following what regional authorities described as a drone attack in the Leningrad region, Russia, November 11, 2026 [Reuters]
Finland’s military says it detected “a strike” on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, as Ukraine sent waves of drones towards Russia’s northwestern Leningrad region.
The strike came as Russian and Ukrainian delegations met in Abu Dhabi for their first United States-brokered talks since February.
It was a rare strike on a Russian navy vessel in the Baltic Sea .
So why is Ukraine taking the war to the Baltic, and why now? Here’s what we know:
“The Finnish Defence Forces detected… a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation,” a military spokesperson told the Reuters news agency in an emailed statement.
The spokesperson said Finland was not under any immediate military threat, but declined to say where or when the incident happened, or how it had been detected.
It was not immediately clear whether there were any casualties. Estonian media reported that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship that later returned to St Petersburg.
On Wednesday, drones also caused a fire in the Russian port area of Ust-Luga, injuring three workers, regional Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania told citizens to take shelter as drones strayed into their airspace, and NATO scrambled warplanes in response.
The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, both NATO members, that extends east to St Petersburg. Ust-Luga, on its southern shore, is a key export outlet for Russian oil and grain.
Several Ukrainian drones deployed towards the Leningrad region have strayed into the airspace of Finland and the Baltic states, raising fears that the war is spilling over into NATO countries that border Russia.
Finland’s Defence Minister Antti Hakkanen said Helsinki had raised the strike with Kyiv.
“We have told the Ukrainians this time, and a little earlier too, how sensitive this narrow stretch of the Gulf of Finland, right between us and Estonia, is in terms of environmental safety and the safety of civilian shipping,” he said, according to Finnish broadcaster Yle.
But he said the spillover effects in the surrounding region stem from Ukraine’s defensive fight and assured the public the Baltic Sea around Finland was still safe.
“You can still cruise with peace of mind,” he said.
Ilya Timtchenko, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defense and Security Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, told Al Jazeera the strike was thought to be the first by Ukrainian forces on a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic used by civilian traffic.
“Ukraine and its European allies are showing that they are unified in their approach to fighting off the Russian threat,” he told Al Jazeera.
Two US Navy Unmanned Surface Vessel (USV) drone boats navigate during a NATO exercise off the coast of Gdynia, Poland [File: Omar Marques/Getty Images] What has Ukraine said?
Ukraine’s Security Service said it attacked the Buyan-M-class small missile ship, Naro-Fominsk, as part of a special operation, according to Yle.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s General Staff said the strike on Ust-Luga had damaged five fuel tanks.
“According to preliminary information, as a result of drone strikes on the port’s oil infrastructure, the tank network suffered the most damage,” it reported on Telegram.
On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Ireland and praised their mediation efforts.
Russia, Ukraine and the US held two days of talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday. The last such talks took place in February this year.
The talks produced no breakthrough, apart from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners. Russia’s state-run TASS news agency said the exchange should happen in two to three weeks.
Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to control all of Ukraine’s Donbas region.
Moscow’s demands reach beyond Ukraine as well, focusing also on the expansion of NATO.
Russian negotiators proposed in Abu Dhabi that Finland, which joined the alliance in 2023, leave NATO and that the alliance be barred from having military bases in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the German newspaper Bild reported on Friday.
The informal proposals, shared with European representatives, also called for arrangements to guarantee freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea, Bild reported.
On Thursday, Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow, where the two sides agreed to continue the talks, before the envoys met Zelenskyy in Ireland.
“Kyiv continues to demonstrate two points simultaneously: That it is willing to negotiate and that it has a position of strength,” Timtchenko said. “In parallel with any peace talks, Ukraine will likely continue to strike Russia’s military and the sources of funding for Russia’s war machine.”
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian refineries, ports, and energy infrastructure to raise the economic cost of Moscow’s war effort.
But the strikes have drawn criticism from Washington. Trump has blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy infrastructure for rising diesel prices, and last month he waived sanctions on Russia that Congress had overwhelmingly approved.
Timtchenko said the strikes still gave Kyiv leverage. “Long-range strikes considerably strengthen Ukraine’s hand at the negotiating table, which is why Russian officials keep bringing them up,” he said.
Russia has not commented publicly on the reported strike on its warship.
Governor Drozdenko said 150 drones were shot down over the Leningrad region during Wednesday’s attack, which also cut off a power station.
“Moscow might voice harsh rhetoric and try to blame the Ukrainians for undermining the peace talks,” Timtchenko said. “However, this is nothing new, since Russia has done this numerous times before.
“Despite Moscow’s pretence of seeking an end to the war, Russia continues to strike Ukraine’s military, critical infrastructure, and civilians,” he added.

items.title: Malaysia committed to strong economic ties with Taiwan while upholding One China Policy, says PM Anwar - Asia News Network
items.summary: Malaysia committed to strong economic ties with Taiwan while upholding One China Policy, says PM Anwar  Asia News Network</f
items.content:
KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia remains committed to maintaining strong economic ties with Taiwan while upholding its recognition of the One China Policy, says Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim.
The Prime Minister said as of Wednesday (Nov 11), there had been no signs of investor flight from Taiwan.
"Taiwan is an important trading partner. Our economic cooperation, trade and investment relations are good, and we want to maintain these positive economic and trade ties,” he said during the Prime Minister’s Question Time in the Dewan Rakyat on Thursday (Nov 12)
However, we cannot contravene the One China Policy. Our recognition is of one China, with its government based in Beijing,” he added.
Anwar said Taiwan had significant investments in projects in Malaysia, including one that is to the tune of close to RM1bil investment in Kedah.
“As far as I am concerned, there have been no problems with Taiwanese investments and business operations to date. Even as of yesterday, there were no issues,” he said.
There are new investments, and discussions are continuing. However, we must distinguish between trade relations, economic cooperation and our positive working relationship with Taiwan,” he added.
He was responding to a question from Datuk Mohd Suhaimi Abdullah (PN-Langkawi) on whether the government could confirm a news report which stated that Taiwan had suspended investment talks with Malaysia following his remarks describing Taiwan as part of China.
He said the One China Policy had been in place since 1974.
“From a policy perspective, I would say that our policy has not changed. Malaysia's policy has remained consistent since 1974, and the current government recognises the One China Policy,” he said.
He said this is also why Malaysia does not have an embassy in Taiwan to this day.
“At most, there is only a trade office. There is no official diplomatic office to this day,” he said.
He also dismissed notions that there were “trade negotiations”, adding that the postponed meeting was that of an Economic Cooperation Committee.
“ The meeting was postponed at the time, and we have now referred the matter back to them, requesting that the meeting be resumed,” he said.
This is the Economic Cooperation Committee, not what was mentioned earlier. There are no negotiations as such. There are, however, a Trade Working Committee and an Investment Working Committee,” he added.
Meanwhile, Anwar also hit back at Datuk Seri Hamzah Zainudin, who questioned why the prime minister needed to “rock the boat” with his remarks on the China-Taiwan issue in a recent interview with Al Jazeera and also that he had supported China’s use of military power against Taiwan.
“What does ‘rock the boat' mean? Listen carefully to my interview. Did I say that I agreed that China should attack Taiwan? No. I said,  we support the One China Policy,” he said.
Secondly, we said, ‘We believe there should be an amicable resolution through peaceful efforts.' Now, the next question is, what if China decides to invade? That is purely a domestic policy matter, and we do not interfere. Please understand the language properly. Listen to it again. Alright,” he added.
Anwar maintained that Malaysia will continue to uphold the One China Policy while also emphasising that relations with Taiwan should continue in terms of trade and investment.

items.title: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
items.summary: The army has taken control of most of Tigray's main towns - it is unclear if the TPLF is capable of fighting back.
items.content:
Image caption, Pro-government forces marched into Tigray's capital less than two weeks after the war began
By Michael Teferi ,Â  BBC Africa Â  and Â  Yemane Nagish ,Â  BBC Tigrinya
Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment.
"People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC.
After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter.
"Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion.
Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next."
Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.
But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force.
Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements.
Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority.
Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat.
"The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage."
Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says.
Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost.
Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC.
Image caption, Dozens of people were killed in drone strikes during the short conflict
He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy."
The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability.
It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored.
Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes.
Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days.
"We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active.
Memories of the devastating 2020-2022 Tigray war remain raw for many residents.
The conflict saw widespread human rights abuses and allegations of ethnic cleansing in Western Tigray, while estimates suggest the war claimed hundreds of thousands of lives.
As soldiers from Eritrea, accused of some of the worst atrocities in the previous conflict, and Ethiopia have reappeared in Tigray's towns, many residents describe a profound sense of fear and anxiety, saying the sight of the troops has reopened still-fresh wounds.
Military sources aligned with the federal army say operations against the TPLF are continuing, with recent fighting and troop movements reported in northern Tigray, near the Eritrean border, as well as across central Tigray's rugged highlands. They claim the TPLF's capabilities are being steadily degraded.
Security analysts and observers agree that unrest is likely to continue for some time. "I see a situation in which there could be a prolonged war in Tigray," Yared Tibebu, a well-known Ethiopian commentator based in the US, tells the BBC.
Yared argues that the TPLF has a long history of waging protracted armed struggles and believes the movement is once again preparing for a lengthy conflict. He believes that once the group has reorganised its military and political structures, it may attempt to resume offensive operations.
However he believes this will not happen for some time because of internal divisions - a suggestion dismissed by TPLF spokesperson Mikael.
Image caption, The army says it seized all these weapons from the TPLF during the fighting
Hudson rejects the idea that Tigray is heading towards a prolonged war but agrees that the region may not be truly peaceful for some time. "The TPLF may continue a low-level insurgency and guerrilla campaign, but that is not war. I do not think there will be a wider-scale conflict between the federal forces and the TPLF."
He says the TPLF no longer possesses the size, strength or military capability required to effectively confront federal forces, which he says have significantly expanded and modernised in recent years. "The TPLF has also lost much of its public support and cannot easily rebuild its ranks through recruitment," he says.
Yared, on the other hand, points to the TPLF's history of overcoming setbacks as evidence that the movement could recover to sustain a prolonged struggle. "The TPLF has overcome many major challenges in the past. It is wrong to conclude that it has no public support. It is a political movement with a history stretching back more than 50 years," he says.
Image caption, Most Mekelle residents only have money for the basic necessities at the moment
What Yared sees as a strength, Hudson sees as a weakness, saying the TPLF is still "trapped in the past", and continues to behave as a dominant party within Tigray, even though the situation has changed. "It is a movement that has not evolved, modernised or expanded."
While Hudson argues that the TPLF is not equipped to sustain a major military campaign, the TPLF spokesman says the group obtains weapons and logistical supplies from the Ethiopian military. "We seize weapons from our enemy, and the weaponry that has entered Tigray will, sooner or later, become ours."
In early October, eyewitnesses told the BBC they had seen Eritrean troops in Tigray amid reports they were backing the TPLF . However, they appear to have returned home and Hudson thinks the country would be wary of becoming further embroiled in the conflict.
"First, Eritrea does not have unlimited resources. Second, the TPLF is no more an effective military force, and Eritrean leaders may have concluded that supporting it at this stage would not yield significant military gains," he says. "Third, Eritrea would have to consider the risk of provoking a confrontation with Ethiopia if it openly backs the TPLF."
Sources in the Ethiopia army tell the BBC that senior members of the TPLF's political leadership were briefly based in Eritrea, however, they say the authorities ordered them to leave in early November, shortly after President Isaias Afwerki returned from Russia. According to the sources, the move was driven by concerns that Ethiopia could use their presence as a reason to invade.
Hudson also argues that Eritrea's renewed diplomatic engagement with the US, whose relations with the TPLF have long been strained, could further discourage Asmara from providing meaningful support to the movement.
In September, seven Ethiopian rebel groups led by the TPLF announced the formation of a new coalition called the Alliance for Survival, aimed at removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.
Figure caption, Seven rebel groups from across Ethiopia have announced a new alliance
Yared believes the alliance could give the TPLF the strength to keep on fighting. "Its members can combine their strengths. The TDF [the TPLF's military wing] has leadership experience and organisational capacity, while Fano [an ethnic Amhara militia] is believed to have between 70,000 and 80,000 fighters.
"If conditions emerge that allow the forces to co-ordinate effectively, the TPLF's current difficulties may not last long," he says.
Hudson, however, rejects that argument, insisting that the alliance is unlikely to alter the balance of power. "I don't think the TPLF can be saved by this alliance. The ethnic militias have not demonstrated the capacity, either individually or collectively, to pose a serious threat to federal forces. We should not underestimate the strength of the federal army," he says.
Abraha from Mekelle University argues that the conflict in Tigray will only truly be over if the federal government addresses the region's feeling that it has been marginalised, both economically and politically by the current government.
However, many Tigrayan elites and political observers remain wary of the federal government's intentions. They question whether the authorities in Addis Ababa are genuinely seeking to address Tigray's problems, or whether they are taking advantage of the region's weakness to boost their influence.
In the meantime, many ordinary people in Tigray say their priority is peace.
"Peace seems slow in coming. Most people are tired of politics. Whatever happens, we only want peace and a chance to rebuild our lives," says Firut from her beauty salon in Mekelle.

items.content:
Chicago Fed's Goolsbee says central bank 'has definitely got work to do' on inflation
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Friday that the central bank is getting further away from its inflation goal and "has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility.
In a CNBC interview, the policymaker indicated that inflation is beginning to spread.
Wage growth is not a leading indicator of inflation: Fed's Goolsbee
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee expressed concern about the latest inflation data, telling CNBC on Friday that the central bank likely will need to take action.
"I believe that the the central bank has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility," the policymaker said during an interview on "Squawk Box."
His remarks came shortly after the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the producer price index , considered a proxy for wholesale prices, posted a 0.3% increase in October, which was slightly less than expected, but also indicated a 6.5% annual gain, the highest since November 2022.
With data in hand earlier in the week showing that the consumer price index rose a bit more than expected during the month, Goolsbee said the Fed is slipping further away from its 2% inflation target.
"We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," he said.
"Inflation is rising. It's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks, and now we're adding this old-fashioned demand overheating coming from the AI data center buildout, that looks like it's starting to spread out of its lane," Goolsbee added.
Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase when the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets next on Dec. 8-9. There also is a better than 10% probability of a half-point hike, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge of futures markets. Goolsbee is not currently an FOMC voter but will be in 2027.
Earlier in the week, Fed Governor Christopher Waller indicated he would entertain a 50 basis point move depending on this week's inflation data.
Goolsbee did not speculate directly on whether the Fed might need to be more aggressive.
"It's it's all going to be about this ... question: What is happening to inflation, and are we on path back to 2%?" he said. "My feeling is, right now we're not."

Storm Charles hits mainland Portugal. Photograph: Filipe Amorim/AFP/Getty Images
Storm Charles hits mainland Portugal. Photograph: Filipe Amorim/AFP/Getty Images
Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week
Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninsula this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours. In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.
After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.
Waves crash into a fort near Estoril as Storm Charles hits mainland Portugal. Photograph: Zed Jameson/Anadolu/Getty Images Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.
Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.
Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.
A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.

Supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October as market shows ‘tentative signs of rebalancing’
The world’s oil supply is swinging back to a surplus for the first time since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has said.
Oil supplies outstripped demand by almost 2m barrels a day in October, the Paris-based agency said, as “Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand”.
The market was “showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran”, the IEA reported.
It comes after months of disruption to the global oil market as the Middle East conflict blocked shipments via the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply normally passes.
The conflict has triggered a rise in energy prices this year. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, traded at about $72 a barrel in February, before the conflict began, and hit $126 a barrel by the end of April.
However, this week prices fell to their lowest level since late August, at $89.66, after the US president, Donald Trump, told reporters that the war with Iran was “ effectively over ”. Brent crude was trading at about $95 a barrel on Friday.
There are still concerns around continued attacks on oil tankers in the Middle East, and this week reports emerged that senior Iranian officials believe the US could be planning further military strikes .
However, the IEA said it expected global oil supply to average 105m barrels a day in the final three months of the year, 1.7m higher than forecast demand. The agency had previously expected a deficit in the fourth quarter.
The recovery in global oil supplies has also eased pressure on emergency stockpiles, which have been diminished by the Iran conflict. The IEA said its members would speed up the release of remaining emergency oil stockpiles pledged earlier this year, adding a further 71m barrels to the market by the end of February. The stocks are held in refineries, oil terminals, power stations and at offshore fields in the North Sea.
The Opec+ oil cartel said this week that it had pumped 41m barrels a day of crude in October, up from about 2m in September and at 97% of its prewar volumes.
Global oil demand is also expected to fall by 2.68m barrels a day this year to 103.2m a day, the IEA reported. Consumption is forecast to rebound next year but is still expected to remain below 2025 levels, with growth mostly in petrochemical feed stocks as the market for vehicle fuel is hit by “high prices, electrification and fuel efficiency”.

S&P 500, Dow, Nasdaq Futures Recover After Markets End Lower On Jensen Huang’s Exit, Oil Price Pressure — CRWV, CBRS, NVDA, TSLA In Focus
The S&P 500 ended Thursday 0.4% lower, the Nasdaq 100 lost 0.3%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.4%.
Super Micro Computer stock tumbled about 11% amid a probe to find out if companies linked to alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang smuggled its products to China.
U.S. stock indices ended lower on Thursday amid a leadership crisis in chipmaker Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down from his position, which weighed on overall tech and AI stocks, while elevated oil prices further bogged down sentiment.
The chief executive of the semiconductor giant resigned from his role after allegations surfaced regarding inappropriate relationships, including an association with an individual suspected by American intelligence of covert ties to Beijing, along with romantic ties with an Nvidia employee.

However, index futures were quick to recover after-hours. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 40 points. S&P 500 futures rose about 0.2%, while Nasdaq-100 futures advanced 0.3% at the time of writing.
The S&P 500 ended Thursday 0.4% lower, the Nasdaq 100 lost 0.3%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.4%. The Russell 2000, which tracks small-cap stocks, ended 1.7% lower.
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) fell 0.4%, and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) lost 0.4%. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ended 0.3% lower on Thursday.
Meanwhile, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and the iShares Semiconductor ETF fell between 0.3% and 1% each on Thursday, mostly pulled down by weakness in Nvidia (NVDA). The broader Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) fell 0.1%.

Nvidia's competitors, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Broadcom (AVGO), rose on Thursday. Fundstrat's Tom Lee stood by his view that technology stocks have already hit bottom. "We are sticking with the thesis that Technology stocks bottomed last week," Lee said on Thursday, in a note cited by CNBC. He added that Huang's exit "does not change our view."
More investors seemed to be of the view that Huang's exit could be a golden opportunity for other chipmakers or firms looking to design their own chips.
"This is a golden opportunity for Amazon, for Google, for AMD, for Broadcom, for OpenAI and Anthropic, who are hiring chip experts to help them design their own chips," Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, told CNBC.
However, the case for AI spending reaching unprecedented levels, creating pressure on cash flows, continued to affect investor sentiment.
"The large technology companies are spending an absolute fortune on AI capex, and I think investors need to be very careful, said Sean Peche, founder and portfolio manager at Ranmore Fund Management.
"Investors tend to assume that what has performed well will continue to do so. History shows that isn't always the case."
Oil prices also jumped on Thursday, further weighing on overall markets after President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post, "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed." U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 2.55% to $88.74 a barrel, while Brent crude futures added 3.3% to $95.82 a barrel.

Federal prosecutors are investigating whether entities linked to Alice Huang were involved in efforts to smuggle Supermicro (SMCI) products into China, according to Bloomberg.
Investor appetite for Anthropic PBC's initial public offering has far outpaced supply , with orders reaching approximately six times the number of shares available, Bloomberg reported.
Shares of Tesla (TSLA) closed higher on Thursday after reports that merger discussions between itself and SpaceX are progressing and could lead to an announcement as soon as December.
Elon Musk's rocket and artificial intelligence company SpaceX (SPCX) said on Thursday that it plans for more than $74 billion in new U.S. supercomputing campuses, pairing a facility at its Starbase site in Texas with a second project in Cochise County in Arizona, as it seeks to expand its AI compute capacity on the ground.

US Stock Futures Edge Lower as Nvidia Leadership Changes Offset Cisco and Applied Materials Forecasts: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Wall Street sign ©Rawpixel US stock index futures traded slightly lower on Friday as investors assessed developments surrounding Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), alongside financial updates from Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) and Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT), disruptions affecting Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) services and movements in commodity markets.
At 03:01 ET (08:01 GMT), Nasdaq 100 futures were down 74 points, or 0.3%, while S&P 500 futures declined five points, equivalent to 0.1%. Dow Jones futures were largely unchanged.
The movements followed the departure of Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang, which has prompted questions about the company's leadership transition and its position in the artificial intelligence semiconductor market.
Nvidia shares declined more than 4% on Thursday after the company announced Huang's departure following reports concerning his personal conduct and alleged connections to individuals associated with Chinese intelligence.
The allegations have also attracted attention from US lawmakers, although the reported claims have not been independently established.
According to Politico, Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott sent letters to Huang and US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick requesting testimony in December concerning companies reportedly involved in transferring Nvidia's advanced processors to China in potential violation of US export restrictions.
Nvidia has begun searching for a permanent chief executive, with Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress appointed to lead the company on an interim basis.
President Donald Trump has also suggested former Apple executive Tim Cook as a possible candidate for the position.
The leadership changes come ahead of Nvidia's scheduled quarterly earnings announcement next week, when investors will receive updated information on the company's financial performance and outlook.
Nvidia's market capitalisation has declined substantially during November, with the source report estimating that the company has lost close to $1 trillion in value during the month.
Elsewhere, Asian equity markets declined, while government bonds in the United States, Japan and Australia also recorded losses.
Oil prices increased following comments from President Trump indicating that Washington no longer considered a peace agreement with Iran necessary.
Cisco Raises Annual Guidance Following Quarterly Revenue Growth
Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) raised its full-year financial outlook after issuing a current-quarter revenue forecast above analysts' expectations.
The networking equipment manufacturer reported fiscal second-quarter revenue of approximately $18.1 billion, exceeding market forecasts.
Cisco's results reflected demand for networking infrastructure used in data centres, including facilities supporting artificial intelligence applications.
The company has been expanding its AI-related networking products while competing with other technology suppliers, including Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Broadcom.
Orders increased 21% compared with the corresponding period a year earlier, although the growth rate moderated from 35% in the preceding quarter.
The company operates in a market where US policymakers are also examining the pace of data centre development, with some Democratic candidates elected during the midterm elections advocating restrictions on further expansion.
Cisco shares declined in extended-hours trading following the announcement.
Applied Materials Forecasts Fiscal First-Quarter Revenue of $11.1 Billion
Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) issued a fiscal first-quarter revenue forecast exceeding analyst expectations, citing continued demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
The California-based company expects revenue of approximately $11.10 billion, with a potential variation of $500 million in either direction.
The forecast compares with the $10.89 billion consensus estimate reported by Reuters, citing LSEG data.
Applied Materials also reported fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of $4.16 per share, exceeding market expectations.
Revenue from its semiconductor systems division increased 64% to $8 billion, contributing to the quarterly performance.
The company supplies manufacturing equipment used by semiconductor producers, including those expanding production capacity for artificial intelligence-related chips.
During the post-results conference call, Chief Executive Gary Dickerson said 2027 would be "another record year for the market and Applied."
Applied Materials shares were slightly lower in after-hours trading, although the stock had gained more than 41% since the beginning of the year.
Microsoft Continues Work to Restore Outlook and Teams Services
Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) said it was continuing efforts to restore access to Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services following a widespread disruption extending into a second day.
The company reported implementing additional measures intended to restore service availability but acknowledged that some changes had not produced the expected results.
"We've monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they're not taking as expected," Microsoft said in a social media update.
Users reported difficulties accessing several Microsoft 365 applications, particularly Outlook and Teams.
The disruptions affected customers across multiple regions, including Asia-Pacific and the Americas.
Microsoft shares declined in premarket trading as the company continued its recovery efforts.
Gold Recovers Above $3,900 as Investors Assess US Interest Rate Outlook
Gold prices increased on Friday after reaching a 13-month low during the previous session, although the metal remained on course for a weekly decline.
Spot gold rose 0.4% to $3,902.22 per ounce, recovering above the $3,900 level.
Despite the daily increase, prices remained more than 4% lower for the week.
The decline followed stronger-than-expected US consumer inflation figures and comments from Federal Reserve officials supporting a more restrictive monetary policy stance.
Higher US Treasury yields and a stronger dollar have also influenced gold prices, as investors reassessed the likelihood of additional interest rate increases.
Market expectations have shifted towards a possible Federal Reserve rate increase in December, with some traders considering the possibility of a 50-basis-point adjustment.
Investors were awaiting Friday's US Producer Price Index report for further information on wholesale inflation and its potential implications for monetary policy.
The release, together with forthcoming Federal Reserve commentary and Nvidia's quarterly results, was expected to remain a focus for financial markets.
